steps.sub: Look at where the -ing word sits in each one.

It is worth trying it ten more times.

steps.title: Look at the first two sentences again.
steps.sub: Liking a food is not a decision. · Eating them is unpleasant.
steps.prompt: What job does the -ing word do here?
options: It is the subject of the sentence — the thing the sentence is about.
It is the main verb of the sentence, in a continuous form.
It describes the noun that comes immediately after it.
steps.answer: It is the subject of the sentence — the thing the sentence is about.
steps.why: An -ing form can act as a noun. A subject like this always takes a singular verb: Cooking is …

steps.title: Where the -ing form is used
steps.html:
Where it goesExample
as the subjectCooking is my favourite way to relax.
after a prepositionI’m interested in learning to cook.
after certain verbsI gave up eating meat. / I don’t mind waiting.
after it’s worth / it’s no useIt’s worth trying it again.
after go for activitiesWe often go shopping on Saturday.
after spend + timeI spend hours cooking at the weekend.

As a subject, the -ing form behaves like a noun and takes a singular verb: Eating them is unpleasant, not are.

After every preposition, use -ing: interested in cooking, good at cooking, before cooking, instead of cooking.

Careful with to: it is usually part of an infinitive (I want to cook), but in look forward to and be used to it is a preposition: I look forward to cooking.

Spelling: cook → cooking, make → making (drop the e), cut → cutting (double the consonant).

You met this form in Lesson 3 (like / love / can’t stand) and in Lesson 10 (verb patterns). This lesson puts all its uses together.

steps.title: Why we like what we like
steps.html:
Taste buds, texture, smell and memory.

Reading

Liking a food is not a decision. It happens before you notice it.

Part of the answer is on your tongue. We all have taste buds, but not the same number of them. About a quarter of people have far more than average. For them, black coffee, dark chocolate and spinach are strongly bitter, and eating them is genuinely unpleasant. Another quarter have very few, and taste almost nothing strongly. Most of us are somewhere in the middle. So when two people argue about whether a dish is too spicy, they may both be telling the truth.

But taste is only part of it. Texture decides more than people admit: many adults who say they hate tomatoes are fine with tomato sauce. And smell does most of the work — without it, an onion and an apple are difficult to tell apart.

The rest is memory. If a food was on the table at home every week, you will probably go on eating it all your life. This is why people who grew up with sour flavours look for them, and why somebody who has never tried a stew with honey in it finds the idea strange.

There is one useful piece of news. Liking is not fixed. Researchers say that most adults start to enjoy a new flavour after about ten or twelve tries — not two. So before you say you don’t like something, it is worth trying it ten more times.

steps.sub: Six sentences. Three describe the dish; three use the -ing form.
steps.html:
1. Plan: what the dish is → what is in it → how it tastes and feels → what you enjoy about cooking or eating → something you gave up → something worth trying.
  • This is a kind of …
  • It’s made with …
  • It tastes … and the texture is …
  • …ing is … for me.
  • I gave up …ing …
  • It’s worth …ing …
